analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to disclose pay ranges in job postings and to current employees.
analysis.headline: The bill, requiring employers to post wage ranges for every job opening, has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee with no hearing or vote since its March 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The Salary Transparency Act would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to make it unlawful for an employer to post a job opening without disclosing the wage or salary range, to discuss compensation with an applicant without first disclosing the range, or to withhold the wage range from a current employee for their own position when hired, at least annually, and on request. It would also make it illegal to retaliate against anyone who asserts these rights, and it would impose a $5,000 civil penalty for a first violation (capped at $10,000 for repeat violations) and let affected workers sue for $1,000 to $10,000 or actual damages, plus attorneys' fees. The bill was introduced in March 2025 and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Job applicants and current employees benefit. Applicants would see the pay range before applying or negotiating, ending the practice of investing time in interviews only to learn the salary is far below expectations. Existing employees would learn the range for their own job at least yearly, giving them leverage in raise negotiations and helping to surface pay gaps between similar workers. Anyone penalized for asking about pay would have legal recourse, including damages and attorneys' fees.

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to include the wage or wage range in any public or internal job posting, and disclose it to any applicant before discussing compensation and on request.
Current employees would be entitled to the wage range for their own position when hired, at least once a year, and anytime on request.
It would be unlawful to refuse to interview, hire, or promote, or otherwise retaliate against, anyone who exercises these rights.

Violations carry a $5,000 civil penalty for a first offense (rising to a $10,000 cap) and give affected workers or applicants the right to sue for $1,000–$10,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorneys' fees.

analysis.who_pays: Employers pay. They would need to establish and document good-faith wage ranges for every position, include them in every public and internal job posting, disclose them to current employees at hire and annually, and face civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation plus individual or class-action damages for failures. Small businesses without formal pay structures would bear relatively heavier administrative burdens, and employers could face pressure to keep openings unfilled rather than post a range that reveals internal inequities.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face real compliance and litigation costs: they would need to set and maintain good-faith wage ranges for every job, disclose them in every posting, and could face $5,000 civil penalties plus statutory damages of $1,000–$10,000 per affected person, with class actions allowed in federal or state court.

The bill defines a 'wage range' flexibly (pay scale, previously determined range, incumbents' range, or budgeted amount), which could let some employers post very broad ranges that convey little actual information, weakening the benefit to workers.

The disclosure requirement applies to every posting for an employment opportunity, including internal ones, which adds administrative burden for employers of any size, with no small-business exemption in the text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: pay transparency has been adopted in a growing number of states and cities, and workers there can see salary ranges before applying or negotiating, which narrows information gaps that especially disadvantage women and people of color. The costs are also real and acknowledged by supporters of such laws: employers must maintain accurate, defensible pay ranges and may face penalties or lawsuits over postings, which falls hardest on small businesses and creates pressure to keep hiring quiet or use broad ranges. On balance the bill is a consumer-protection-style rule for the labor market — low burden on honest employers, meaningful leverage for workers — but it adds a new compliance and litigation surface, and it would do nothing to change the underlying pay itself, only the visibility of it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee in March 2025, and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no vote, and it was never brought to the House floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 10, 2025, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
No further action has been taken: the committee has not held a hearing or vote, and the bill has not reached the House floor.
Nearly all pay-transparency bills introduced in Congress in recent years have died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that prefer not to disclose pay are better off so far, since the bill has not advanced and workers have gained nothing from it. Whether that holds depends on whether the committee acts before the Congress ends in early 2027.

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Delegate, District of Columbia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 10, 2025 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee (unspecified chair)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: The committee has not held a hearing or markup on the bill since its referral, the step that is required before a bill can move to the floor.

against.name: Employer and small-business groups
against.what_they_did: Business groups have historically opposed federal pay-transparency mandates, citing compliance costs and litigation exposure; no specific recorded action on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: Both cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a non-voting Democratic delegate; no Republicans have signed on, though no vote has occurred to reveal where members stand.

industries.note: Every employer would have to post wage ranges for job openings, disclose ranges to current employees annually, and absorb penalties and potential class-action liability for failures. Honest, well-structured employers would face modest compliance costs; opaque payers would lose their main negotiating advantage.

industries.industry: Human resources software and job-posting platforms
industries.note: Job boards and HR systems would need to build wage-range fields into postings, a modest compliance-driven demand for their services.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has seen no committee action since referral in March 2025. A first-term bill from a non-voting delegate with two cosponsors and no Republican support is very unlikely to get a hearing in the Education and Workforce Committee, let alone a floor vote; the most probable outcome is that it dies quietly when this Congress ends in January 2027, like most pay-transparency proposals, unless similar state laws build broader momentum for federal action.
